source.title: Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions: A Theory of Generalization, Weights Spectra, and Scaling Laws
source.authors: Fabrizio Boncoraglio; Vittorio Erba; Emanuele Troiani; Yi-Zhou Xu; Florent Krzakala; Lenka Zdeborová

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and reports sample-size scaling laws for test error in a synthetic attention model, including multiple scaling regimes whose behavior depends on target spectrum and regularization. This refines the claim about power-law curve shapes, but it does not test language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own theoretical and numerical sample-size scaling results for excess test error. Results cited from other studies are excluded. Other reported comparisons, such as factorized versus non-factorized training, do not measure the scaling-law claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a solvable-model theory paper. It derives and simulates test-error power laws in sample count for a synthetic single-head tied-attention layer trained by ERM on Gaussian inputs, at d = 200 in the numerical checks. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It fits no laws to small runs to extrapolate, studies no compute-optimal split, compares no architectures at fixed parameter count, and examines no published-law disagreement or fitting choices. Its multi-regime exponents are analytic properties of a toy matrix-sensing-like estimator, not evidence about the kind of system any version names. Its relation to the claim is a proposed mechanism for scaling laws, so it falls under fits_no_version. The record's T5 is wrong: the paper argues no version is wrong or partial.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors give an exact high-dimensional theory of single-head tied attention covering train/test error, thresholds and weight spectra. For power-law targets, they say modes are recovered sequentially, producing emergence and power-law test-error scaling in n. The rates match LASSO/matrix-sensing rates and, at optimal regularization, the minimax rate n^{−1+1/(2γ)}. They flag isotropic data, tied single-head attention and the asymptotic limit as limitations. They make no claim about LM pretraining scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Unlike the cited language-model scaling studies, this paper analyzes tied single-head attention trained by ERM on synthetic supervised tasks, and studies test error versus sample number and regularization rather than held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling rates vary with target-spectrum exponent γ, regularization λ, and sample/dimension regime. In additional experiments, matched softmax temperature affects test error, while curves for different token counts largely align after rescaling the sample ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: In a high-dimensional single-head tied-attention ERM model with a power-law target spectrum, excess test error decays as a power of sample number n. The exponent depends on the target decay γ and on the regularization/sample regime, giving several regimes with crossovers. Under optimal regularization it reaches n^{−1+1/(2γ)}, the LASSO minimax rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Solvable attention models reproduce sample-size power laws whose exponents are set by target-spectrum decay and regularization, via sequential spectral recovery (a mechanism for scaling laws rather than an LM test).

record.problems: The analysis assumes isotropic data, tied single-head attention, and a high-dimensional limit. The extension of the asymptotic characterization to the finite-size regimes used for some scaling claims is explicitly an assumption/conjecture rather than rigorously controlled. Numerical examples use synthetic tasks and limited simulation instances.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted for the tested version. Findings about architecture comparisons, temperature effects, and token-count rescaling were not extracted because they do not directly measure the scaling-curve or exponent dependence named by V7.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: no depth/width/shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All: no image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. The synthetic regression setting is a theory model, not a tested training regime of real models.
All: no comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules, or disagreement between published LM laws.

record.verdict_notes: Theory and toy-model paper. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as motivation. The finite-size extension behind the scaling results is stated as a conjecture (Appendix E). Rows R6 and R7 transcribe Eq. 25 incorrectly; see row_fixes. No verdict labels are given because no row measures what any version names.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, or training compute.
Whether laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream-task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study does not compare Kaplan and Hoffmann compute-optimal fits, test choices such as parameter counting or training schedule, or establish disagreement between published language-model laws. Its setup-dependence evidence concerns synthetic attention test error, target-spectrum decay, and regularization.

reader_labels.condition: Synthetic single-head tied-attention ERM with power-law target spectra, across the reported sample-size and regularization regimes
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports distinct power-law rates across regimes and different decay exponents for different regularization settings; the numerical curves are described as having multiple scaling regimes (R1–R7).
